issues.legal_issue: A High Court may entertain a writ challenge to an insolvency tribunal’s order despite an available statutory appeal when the tribunal acted without jurisdiction by reviewing a public-law administrative decision.
material_facts: During the corporate insolvency resolution process, the State refused to extend a corporate debtor’s mining lease, citing alleged breaches of the lease and statutory rules.
The resolution professional challenged the State’s refusal before the insolvency tribunal, which set aside the refusal and directed the State to execute supplemental lease deeds.
The State challenged the tribunal’s order by writ petition instead of pursuing the statutory appeal, and the High Court stayed the tribunal’s direction.
The tribunal’s order concerned the State’s exercise of statutory authority over a mining lease on State land, rather than a matter within the tribunal’s insolvency jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The tribunal lacked jurisdiction to direct the State to extend the mining lease, so the High Court was justified in entertaining the writ petition despite the available appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 permits public-law review, and the availability of a statutory appeal ordinarily counsels against a writ petition. However, the distinction between an authority acting without jurisdiction and wrongly exercising jurisdiction it possesses remains relevant when deciding whether an alternative remedy may be bypassed. Under Sections 60(5) and 63 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, the insolvency tribunal’s jurisdiction does not extend to reviewing a government or statutory authority’s public-law decision under the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act. The Court relied on Official Trustee, West Bengal v. Sachindra Nath Chatterjee, Anisminic Ltd. v. Foreign Compensation Commission, Union Bank of India v. Satyawati Tandon, Sadhana Lodh v. National Insurance Co., Nivedita Sharma v. Cellular Operators Association of India, and Cicily Kallarackal v. Vehicle Factory, among other authorities.

rule.if: writ_challenge_to_tribunal_order and statutory_appeal_available and tribunal_order_reviewed_public_law_action and tribunal_lacked_power_to_review_administrative_action

predicates.writ_challenge_to_tribunal_order: A party challenged an insolvency tribunal’s order by seeking public-law review in a High Court.
predicates.statutory_appeal_available: The governing process provided an appeal from the tribunal’s order to a statutory appellate tribunal.
predicates.tribunal_order_reviewed_public_law_actio: The tribunal set aside or reviewed a government or statutory authority’s administrative decision.
predicates.tribunal_lacked_power_to_review_administ: The tribunal had no authority to review that kind of administrative decision.

issues.definition: When a party seeks review of a tribunal order, an available statutory appeal does not prevent the High Court from entertaining a writ if the tribunal reviewed public-law action it had no power to review.

issues.legal_issue: An insolvency tribunal may inquire into allegations that insolvency proceedings were initiated fraudulently, and those allegations alone do not justify bypassing the statutory appeal.
material_facts: The State alleged that the insolvency process had been initiated collusively for a purpose other than resolving insolvency, including to obtain the benefit of the mining lease.

The State alleged that individuals and entities connected with the corporate debtor, the initiating creditor, and the resolution applicant had overlapping relationships and roles in agreements and communications concerning the debtor.
The State relied on those allegations when choosing to challenge the tribunal’s order by writ petition rather than appeal to the appellate tribunal.
The insolvency legislation provides for inquiry and penalties concerning fraudulent or malicious initiation of proceedings and fraudulent transactions.
issues.conclusion: The insolvency tribunal and its appellate tribunal have jurisdiction to inquire into allegations of fraudulent initiation; such allegations alone do not permit a party to bypass the statutory appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 65 and 66 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code address fraudulent or malicious initiation of proceedings and fraudulent transactions, while Section 69 addresses specified fraudulent conduct by corporate debtors and their officers. These provisions place inquiry into such matters within the adjudicating authority’s jurisdiction. Accordingly, allegations of fraudulent initiation do not, by themselves, displace the appeal provided by Section 61.

rule.if: insolvency_resolution_proceeding and challenge_to_tribunal_order and statutory_appeal_available and fraudulent_initiation_alleged

predicates.insolvency_resolution_proceeding: A proceeding was initiated to resolve a corporate debtor’s insolvency.
predicates.challenge_to_tribunal_order: A party challenged an order made in the insolvency proceeding.
predicates.statutory_appeal_available: The governing process provided an appeal from the challenged order to a statutory appellate tribunal.
predicates.fraudulent_initiation_alleged: A party alleged that the insolvency proceeding was initiated fraudulently or for a collateral purpose rather than genuine insolvency resolution.

issues.definition: When a tribunal order in an insolvency proceeding is challenged and an appeal is available, an allegation of fraudulent initiation can be considered by the insolvency tribunals but does not alone justify bypassing that appeal.

issues.legal_issue: A moratorium during corporate insolvency preserves the existing position but does not create or compel renewal of an expiring government mining lease.
material_facts: A corporate debtor held a mining lease over State land that was due to expire while its corporate insolvency resolution process was underway.
The State refused the requested deemed extension, citing alleged breaches of the lease and statutory rules.
The resolution professional argued that the moratorium prevented the State’s decision and supported continuation of the lease.
The lease granted mining rights for a specified period and did not give the debtor exclusive possession of the leased area.
issues.conclusion: The moratorium did not affect the State’s right to refuse an extension and did not create a right to renewal of the lease.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code operates to preserve the status quo; it does not create a new right. The protection against recovery of property under Section 14(1)(d) concerns the right not to be dispossessed and does not confer a right to renewal of a lease, particularly where the grant is a time-limited mining right rather than exclusive possession.

predicates.corporate_insolvency_moratorium_applies: A corporate debtor was subject to a moratorium during an insolvency resolution process.
predicates.debtor_seeks_continuation_of_expiring_pu: The debtor or its representative sought to continue a government mining lease that was due to expire.
predicates.state_refused_lease_extension: The government refused to extend the mining lease.

issues.definition: When a debtor under a moratorium seeks continuation of an expiring government mining lease that the government has refused to extend, the moratorium does not create or compel renewal.
